newsitem.title: INDIA: India ICICI profit growth seen slowing.
newsitem.headline: India ICICI profit growth seen slowing.

text.p: Term lender Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (ICICI) is likely to show a slowdown in profit growth for the year ended March 31, 1997, banking analysts said on Friday.
ICICI, India's second largest term lending bank, announces its results for 1996/97 (April/March) on Monday.
The slowdown in profit growth may continue for the next years, analysts said.
ICICI is likely to report a 1996/97 (April-March) net profit between 6.6 billion rupee and 6.7 billion, analysts said.
They said spreads would be lower but volume growth would help ICICI post growth in profits, although the rate of growth would be less than last year.
"ICICI, after merging with SCICI, should show a profit after tax of around 6.6 billion rupees against 6.14 last year," said Amit Rajpal, banking analyst at Prime Broking.
This was an increase of around 7.0 percent over the previous year, he said.
ICICI had shown a 21 percent growth in net profit in 1995/96 but that was before it was merged with SCICI.
ICICI and another term lender SCICI were merged last year with effect from April 1, 1996.
"Margins will have dropped but a growth in volumes will help increase profits," Rajpal said.
He said he expected a growth in volume of around 20 percent over the 1995/96 figure.
S.R Krishnan, banking analyst at Peregrine capital India, said he expected ICICI to post a net profit of 6.6 billion rupees.
"I expect margins to have fallen from 1995/96 but the inflow of funds through GDRs should cushion the fall," he said.
ICICI raised $230 million through an issue of global depositary receipts last August.

Analysts said this would have provided the corporation with a source of cheap funds and mitigated the effect of high cost of rupee borrowings and poor yield on rupee loans last year. "There were times last year when ICICI borrowed funds from the market at rates exceeding its prime lending rate," Rajpal said.
"I expect spreads to some down to 2.2 percent from 2.6," he said. "This is on account of higher cost of rupee borrowings and lower yield on its own rupee loans."
Rajpal said he expected a growth in net profit of around 5.0 percent in 1997/98.
He said he expected spreads to continue dropping over the next two years.
"Volume growth may also be less next year as banks start competing in the term lending market," Rajpal said.
